doc.title: Keter Betts interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 11, 1996

title: Playing for the audience and music as a language
summary: On connecting with listeners, originality, Cannonball's philosophy, and music as a universal language and a prayer of thanks.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: I really like it when a musician seems to — what they’re thinking seems to connect with the audience. Like last night when you were doing a solo and — I can’t remember which tune it was — and you were doing a sliding —

And when you got about into the fourth measure, people, I could tell people were like with you. They thought they knew what you were going to do. And you almost did it, except that you would change it a little bit. But you could feel it around me, like yeah, I like this thing he’s doing.

Well you’re playing for the public, I mean you’re playing for yourself, you’re playing for the musicians but you’re playing for the public because these are the ones who came to see you. And you take your ability, what you have, and utilize it to the best that you can. And this is where judgment comes in, and this is where originality comes in also. You
know it’s like writing a book or some novel. I mean everybody knows words, but it’s how good an author can put these words together to make it interesting.

Cannonball had a particular philosophy on that too. I just read an article about him and he was saying how it’s kind of a balance between keeping your own originality but you’re playing for the public and you’re there to please them.

Well, one of the things that I’ve found over the course of the years with all of the traveling that I’ve done throughout the world is that music is a language within itself. And when you forget about speaking words, which English is here and there and there is all other different languages, but the music itself has its own language that people understand and comprehend — if they like it or if it’s good. And I think that when you speak music, and you speak music from your mind, people understand it. Your mouth can be running a mile a minute, if you’re not saying nothing, it doesn’t mean nothing. But if you’re speaking music, then, because your whole purpose is to make people happy and make yourself happy too. So I consider it to a certain point, as they say, if they have the gods to give you talent of whatever field that you’re in, and so when you’re taking a solo it’s like you’re saying a little prayer, thanking Him for the ability to be able to do this. Make sense?
Not too heavy for you this early in the morning?
